definition: A model trained on huge amounts of text that generates replies by repeatedly predicting a likely next token. It produces plausible text; it doesn't look facts up.
The unit an LLM reads and writes: a word or part of a word. Limits and speeds (context window, max tokens, tokens per second) are measured in tokens.
The text sent to the model: the system prompt plus the conversation so far.
Hidden instructions the app gives the model before the user's messages: the bot's persona, scope and facts. For testers it's the closest thing to a specification.
Everything the model can see at once: the system prompt and the conversation. It has a size limit, so long conversations can push early messages out.
A setting for how random the model's word choices are. 0 is the most predictable; around 0.7–1 is typical for chatbots.
A number that fixes the model's random choices. Same model, conversation, temperature and seed give the same reply, which makes bugs reproducible.
The same input can produce different outputs. Normal for chatbots; testers check that the meaning, facts and decisions stay consistent even when wording changes.
When a model states something false or made up as if it were true: invented facts, sources, URLs, prices or policies.
Giving the model trusted information (such as the client's policies or documents) to base its answers on, and checking it sticks to it.
The character and tone a bot is told to use, such as "cheerful assistant for Sunny Paws". Part of what testers check against the spec.
Input that makes a model follow instructions other than the ones its developers gave it. A top security risk for LLM applications.
A prompt-injection attempt aimed at getting around a model's safety rules.
A bot revealing information it shouldn't: internal notes, system prompts, other customers' data or secrets.
A defence around a model, such as input or output filters, or rules in the system prompt. No single guardrail is complete, which is why they're tested.
A bot refusing a harmless request because it looks similar to a harmful one. A usability bug, just as unsafe answers are a safety bug.
Replies that treat people differently based on name, gender, age, ethnicity or similar, when nothing else has changed.
An automatic pass/fail check on a reply, such as "contains 30" or "matches this pattern". Good chatbot assertions check key facts, not exact sentences.
A saved test re-run after changes (a new prompt, model or setting) to catch behaviour that used to work and now doesn't.
A test that passes on some runs and fails on others with no change. For chatbots, either the bot is inconsistent or the check is too strict.
The written criteria an LLM judge grades against, ideally one specific, checkable criterion per line.
Using one model to grade another model's replies against a rubric. Scales to thousands of replies, but the judge makes mistakes too and needs spot-checking.
